title: The Wallet Firewall: Why 63% of Shoppers Trust AI to Pick Brands but Only 20% Trust It to Spend

html:
The Wallet Firewall: Why 63% of Shoppers Trust AI to Pick Brands but Only 20% Trust It to Spend

A September 2026 Spreedly survey of 2,000 U.S. adults found something that should reshape how we think about agent commerce: 63% of shoppers would let an AI assistant pick their brands for a guaranteed 20% saving, but only 20% would let it spend money without prior approval.

The gap between those numbers is 43 points. That gap has a name: the wallet firewall.

Fraud is the reason

When asked why they hesitate, 52% of respondents named fraud as their top concern, ahead of distrust of AI companies and fear of overspending. This is not abstract anxiety. Shoppers understand intuitively what the industry is still formalizing: letting an agent choose is low-stakes, letting it transact is not.

The agent proposes. Something checks. Money moves only with a gate in between.

Visa's own product lead put it bluntly: agents bring shoppers, but merchants must close the sale. In a PYMNTS interview, Visa's Pavan HS described how the Trusted Agent Protocol hands the merchant the read on an AI agent: origin, intent, and the consumer behind it, so a store can let one browse without letting it check out. The credential only works where the intent allows.

What the wallet firewall actually needs to verify

A firewall that just says "approved" is not a firewall. The check has to answer three questions:

  1. Who is the agent? Is this a legitimate shopping assistant or a compromised session? Know-your-agent verification answers this with cryptographic identity, not vibes.
  1. Who is the counterparty? Is the merchant, seller, or recipient who they claim to be? Counterparty screening checks the other side of the transaction against threat intelligence.
  1. Can anyone prove the check happened? A verdict without a receipt is a claim. Signed, tamper-evident receipts turn "we checked" into "here is the proof."

Most agent-commerce infrastructure today answers zero of these. Payment rails move money. Identity layers verify humans. Nobody verifies the agent-counterparty pair at transaction time.

The 43-point gap is the product

That gap between "pick my brands" and "spend my money" is not a problem to solve with better UX. It is the market telling us exactly what it wants to buy: a trust layer that sits between agent intent and money movement.

The companies that build the wallet firewall own the chokepoint of agent commerce. Every transaction flows through the gate. Every gate needs a verdict. Every verdict needs a receipt.

RelayShield is building exactly this: TAP-based agent identity verification, counterparty screening against a live threat-intel corpus, and signed verdict receipts that prove the check happened. The agent proposes, we check both sides, money moves only on ALLOWED.

The survey says shoppers are ready. The infrastructure is catching up.
